question: Portfolio manager says fund returned 18% CAGR over 10 years. What bias to suspect?
before: Survivorship bias. Fund survived 10 years (probably performed well). Funds that underperformed and were merged/closed are invisible. The 18% figure only looks at the winner. A, C, D are real biases but do not address data selection issue.
after:
Concept: Survivorship bias occurs when analysis includes only entities that have 'survived' a selection process, while excluding those that failed or were eliminated, thereby skewing results toward success.

Why this is correct: When a portfolio manager reports an 18% CAGR over 10 years, that fund is by definition still in existence. All funds that underperformed, were liquidated, merged into other funds, or shut down during that period are absent from the data. The 18% figure therefore reflects only the winners, not the true distribution of returns across all funds that existed at the start. This is the textbook definition of survivorship bias—the sample is contaminated because failures are invisible.

Why the others are wrong: Anchoring bias (A) occurs when an investor fixates on an initial reference point (like a stock's purchase price) and fails to adjust; it does not address the selection of data itself. Confirmation bias (C) is the tendency to seek out information that confirms existing beliefs; while a manager might highlight the 18% to confirm their skill, the bias in question is about which funds appear in the dataset, not how investors interpret it. Recency bias (D) is overweighting recent events in judgment; the 10-year history explicitly counters a recency-only narrative, so this is not the primary concern.

Intuition: Survivorship bias is the most dangerous trap in retrospective fund performance analysis. An analyst comparing fund families must always ask: who is missing from this comparison. The funds you do not see often teach louder lessons than the ones you do. Always adjust for funds that closed, merged, or were spun off to get a true picture of track record credibility.
